content: Stimulus deprivation amblyopia (SDA) arises when there is an obstruction to the passage of light to the retina, such as in cases of cataract. This obstruction prevents the formation of a clear image on the retina, which can result in amblyopia that is often resistant to treatment and associated with a poor visual prognosis. SDA is estimated to account for less than 3% of all amblyopia cases, though precise prevalence rates remain unknown. In high-income countries, most cases are identified in children under the age of one, whereas in lowto middle-income countries, individuals are typically older at the time of diagnosis. The primary treatment approach involves addressing the underlying obstruction, such as surgically removing a cataract, followed by occlusion therapy, where the better-seeing eye is covered to stimulate the weaker eye. However, treatment regimens vary widely, can be challenging to implement, and are traditionally thought to yield suboptimal results. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of occlusion therapy for SDA, to establish realistic treatment outcomes, to investigate any dose-response relationship, and to evaluate how factors such as the duration of treatment, severity of the condition, and the underlying cause influence treatment outcomes. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase, was conducted without restrictions on date or language. The last search was performed on December 12, 2018. The inclusion criteria specified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or controlled clinical trials involving participants with unilateral SDA and visual acuity worse than 0.2 LogMAR or its equivalent. There were no restrictions based on age, gender, ethnicity, comorbidities, medication use, or sample size. Despite using standard Cochrane methodology for data collection and analysis, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. Consequently, no evidence from RCTs or quasi-randomized trials was found to support the effectiveness of any treatment for SDA. The authors concluded that there is a critical need for RCTs to evaluate the safety and efficacy of occlusion therapy for SDA. Future research should aim to determine the realistic visual outcomes achievable, the impact of factors such as age at onset and severity of visual impairment, the optimal occlusion regimen, and the variables associated with both successful and unsuccessful treatment outcomes.
